message.content:
On the lateral chest X-ray, there is increased opacity and blunting of the posterior costophrenic angle with obscuration of the posterior hemidiaphragm. The "spine sign" (increasing density of lower thoracic vertebrae) is present, indicating basilar pathology. In a standard lateral view, the left hemidiaphragm is typically positioned slightly higher than the right; however, the opacity here extends to the most dependent posterior aspect and obscures the lower thoracic spine, which is classically associated with **left** lower lobe atelectasis or consolidation when the left hemidiaphragm silhouette is lost. Right lower lobe atelectasis often presents with a more distinct triangular opacity against the spine but may spare the extreme posterior sulcus if small. Given the diffuse basal opacification and loss of the posterior diaphragmatic contour on this single lateral view, left base atelectasis is the more consistent finding.

Uncertainty: Moderate. Definitive laterality assessment on a single lateral view without a PA correlate is inherently limited, as overlapping structures can mimic contralateral pathology. However, the pattern favors the left side.
